problems.source_says: The scored outcome is cosine similarity between a story's nine binary genre indicators and the average indicators of other stories in its condition. It is not a count of categories, ideas, or unique ideas as category_count is defined in the codebook. The form's measure_detail correctly describes the calculation, but calling category_count the closest vocabulary category does not establish that the coded measure is a count. The codebook supplies no exact type for this categorical-vector similarity; retain the actual calculation and leave the type unresolved rather than asserting a count.
problems.quote: Genre similarity was calculated using cosine similarity between each story's genre vector
problems.locator: PDF p. 16, Figure 4B caption; creativity-codebook.md, section 6, Measure.

problems.source_says: The measure counts genre categories represented within one participant's story. Under the screening rule that within-person variety is flexibility, this is flexibility, not other. The form adds a requirement that categories must occur among multiple separately produced ideas to qualify; neither the within-person-variety rule nor the source establishes that restriction. The with_ai question, category_count measure, and output unit remain appropriate.
problems.quote: GPT-4o was used to classify all stories into one or more of nine popular literary fiction genres (26). Greater AI involvement increased the number of genres per story.
problems.locator: PDF p. 6, Content Diversity, first paragraph; creativity-codebook.md, section 6, Construct, and the brief's within-person-variety rule.

problems.source_says: Figure 4A reports the marginal percentage of stories assigned to each genre and changes in those percentages. This identifies which genres writers choose; it does not itself score how similar different people's outputs are. The source separately introduces genre similarity in Figure 4B to assess variance of genre composition. Merely pooling stories into condition-level percentages does not support classifying the genre-choice outcome as diversity. If retained separately, the supported coding is other/with_ai; S1-O7 already captures the across-person genre-similarity outcome.
problems.quote: Genre distributions across AI assistance types are shown as percentages (above), with differences from non-AI writing displayed as percentage point changes (below).
problems.locator: PDF p. 16, Figure 4A caption; PDF p. 6, Content Diversity, second and third paragraphs; creativity-codebook.md, sections 1 and 6.

confirmed: Criterion 3 holds: two internal and two external evaluators rated the completed story texts, with writer identity and condition hidden. These are output evaluations, not writers' self-assessments (PDF pp. 4, 19, 21; rubric on p. 41).

S1-O1: overall quality integrates creative, interesting, well-written, and coherent expression, supporting the holistic overall_creativity coding and human_raters measure (PDF p. 21, A.2.2; p. 41, B.4 Q7).
S1-O2: originality explicitly asks about novel themes, plot/setting, structure, ending, style, and emotional tone, supporting novelty and human_raters (PDF p. 41, B.4 Q3).
S1-O3: interestingness rates immersion and engagement; other and human_raters accurately describe this separate output criterion (PDF p. 22, A.2.2; p. 41, B.4 Q4).
S1-O4 and S1-O5 rate language quality and organization/coherence, respectively, supporting usefulness and human_raters (PDF p. 22, A.2.2; p. 41, B.4 Q5-Q6).

S1-O1 through S1-O5: rating is the stated unit of the main regressions; 2,196 is the total evaluations per metric across both days, as the form explains (PDF p. 11, Table 1; p. 23, A.3; p. 48, Table S4; p. 51, Table S7).

S1-O1 correctly distinguishes participant-level averaged quality in Table S8 from evaluation-level models in Tables S7 and S9; the recorded adjusted coefficients and standard errors match (PDF pp. 23, 51-53).

All S1 final-story outcomes concern Day 2 production with ChatGPT available. Human Creativity uses AI for drafting/editing after unaided ideation; Day 1 is an earlier no-AI baseline, not after_ai (PDF p. 4, protocol; p. 19, Day 1 and Day 2 tasks).

S1-O6: cosine similarity compares each story embedding with the mean embedding of other stories in its condition using text-embedding-3-large; diversity, across_people, embedding_similarity, and output are supported (PDF pp. 6-7; p. 16, Figure 4C caption).

S1-O7: the comparison is between different writers' stories, with one similarity score per story; diversity, across_people, and output are supported despite the measure-type problem (PDF p. 6; p. 16, Figure 4B caption).

S1-O8 is an automated count of genres assigned to a final story by GPT-4o, supporting scored_on_output, category_count, output, and with_ai; the corpus total is 549 stories, including 278 on Day 1 and 271 on Day 2 (PDF pp. 6, 21).

S1-O9 summarizes GPT-4o genre classifications as condition-level distributions, supporting its descriptive set unit and output basis; the percentages and percentage-point labels match Figure 4A, including the printed -0 values (PDF p. 6; p. 15, Figure 4A, visually checked; p. 16, caption).
All reported quality regression coefficients, standard errors, and significance markers match Tables S4 and S7; reversed contrast orientations are explicitly identified in the form (PDF pp. 48, 51).
All recorded originality, interestingness, writing-quality, and coherence bar labels match Figure 2C; the stated directions in Figure 2A also match (PDF p. 13, Figure 2A and 2C, visually checked).

All recorded semantic-similarity, genre-similarity, and genres-per-story means and confidence limits match the source text, including the pooled Day 1 baselines (PDF pp. 6-7, Content Diversity; Figure 4B-C on pp. 15-16).
The five overall quality-metric means and standard deviations in measure_detail match Table 1 and describe evaluations, not participant-level variation (PDF p. 11, Table 1).

S2-O1: DAT is a computed verbal-creativity score on a generated word list; participants transcribed their first test score rather than supplying a subjective creativity rating. The output unit, overall_creativity construct, and automated_score measure are supported (PDF pp. 19, 21, 35).

S2-O1 compares autonomous ChatGPT tests with unassisted human baseline DAT, so question=none keeps it outside the three assistance questions; mixed denotes those distinct output sources, not an assisted-human DAT condition (PDF p. 8, Discussion; pp. 19, 35, DAT procedure).
S2-O1 reported values match: model mean 85.7, range 82-88, twenty tests; discussion human mean 82.2 and range 65-95; Table 1 human N=280, mean 82.28, SD=7.13 (PDF pp. 8, 11).

After reading the full markdown through SI References, no additional qualifying output outcome was found. Completion time, satisfaction/process flexibility, and reflective-feedback topics are self-reports; quality heterogeneity reuses overall quality (PDF pp. 21-23, 38-44, 45-57).
summary: Criterion 3 holds, and the reported numerical values match the PDF. Three coding problems remain: genre cosine similarity is not a category count, within-story genre variety is flexibility, and genre prevalence alone does not establish across-person diversity.
